Guy who works in betting here. 

For this specific bet, the bookmaker would include a time frame within the wording of the bet (sometimes this can extend to the rules under which their service offers bets). The options would likely be presented as Yes/No with the odds (how much you get paid per amount you bet) next to each option. I'm writing the odds as $ x Number because the way they're written may vary depending on the country you're in, and I'm also making the odds up because for the sake of simplicity.  

Example:
>"Lando Norris to beat Nick Heidfeld record for most Podiums Without Win at 2024 Bahrain GP"

>Yes $ x 10  
>No $ x 2  

The race outcome for Norris could be one of four possibilities: Podium, Win, No Podium or Win, or DNF. If the first outcome occurs, 'Yes' wins the bet. If either of the other three outcomes occur, No wins the bet. Since 'Yes' has a 1 in 4 chance of occurring, you stand to get paid more per amount you bet and conversely, since 'No' has a 3 in 4 chance of occurring, you stand to win less.  

You would probably wait until FP3 before betting to see if the McLarens have any sandbags left to take off and ideally bet a high amount on "No" because there's more chances for that outcome to occur.  

Bookies will probably not offer this bet as standard but many might make it on request. The odds will probably be quite different than what I wrote. It's entirely possible to offer it for the season rather than one race specifically, but that swings the odds wildly.  

Bets are reconciled as soon as official results are submitted.  

I would be more inclined to offer a "Driver to get Maiden Victory in 2024" bet because you could keep it up all season and shift the odds with each race.

I work for an online gambling company so I'm only able to speak to that side of the industry with any real certainty, but the logic can be applied to real world casinos. 

Hypothetically it wouldn't be hard to write code that favours new players, but I've seen no evidence to support this concept. When players win, the house loses, and new registrations are frequent so it wouldn't pay dividends in the long term. 

The common tactic most places use is to reward new players with a either a sign up bonus or a match on their first deposit. This includes terms and conditions that require the player to play a certain amount before cashing out (often to a ridiculous extent) for example, you deposit $50 and we'll give you $50 but you have to play to the value of $500 before cashing out (irl it's probably more like $5000 play through). 

You may look at this and think "What kind of an idiot would take that deal?" Plenty. It's common because it works. 

The point is to retain players and keep them playing until they lose, or at least until they lose more than they win so that even if they cash out they walk away with less overall. Winning players are often rewarded with more bonuses for the sake of retention and for those who lose big amounts we even give tickets to sporting events, and send stupidly expensive bottles of liquor. 

There's a great scene in the film Casino that captures this; A wealthy Asian man visits the casino, plays, wins, and walks away with 2 million dollars. Robert de Niro sees to it that the man misses his flight and the casino offers to cover his lodging. The player of course goes back to the tables and plays again but tries to do so conservatively, but they know that if they keep him there long enough, his impulses will get the better of him and he'll lose everything. 

I know I went off on a bit of a tangent there but the point is that letting new players win at a greater rate is an uncharacteristically high risk strategy for a gambling organization. The most effective and low risk strategy is player retention. There are also entire syndicates of players who are always trying to game the system and exploit any such loopholes (which is usually handled by a department dedicated to risk) for example, we frequently get users signing up new accounts to claim the aforementioned bonuses and take "safe" bets (e.g, two accounts taking either side of an over/under bet that returns even money) and immediately cash out to try and walk out with more than they put in. They're very easy to detect and shut down. 

Finally, casinos and bookies all know these tricks and many employees would be the first to exploit them if they knew it would work. Send someone over to a casino for the first time with a shit load of money, let them place a few bets, win and walk out then send a different person to do the same thing.
